newsitem.title: USA: Raytheon to buy Texas Instruments unit.
newsitem.headline: Raytheon to buy Texas Instruments unit.

text.p: Raytheon Co. said Monday it has a definitive agreement to buy Texas Instruments Inc.'s missile and defence business for $2.95 billion in cash.

The acquisition -- Raytheon's third in the past two years -- strengthens the company's leadership in defence electronics as it seeks to grow further in an industry that has been consolidating for four years since the end of the Cold War.

The deal is expected to increase Raytheon's annualized defence electronics sales to $8 billion and its current defence electronics backlog to $9.3 billion, boosting total annualized revenues to about $15 billion.

"We have consistently said that we will remain a top-tier player in the defence industry," Raytheon Chairman and Chief Executive Dennis Picard said in a statement. "We are buying a growing, world-class business that competes successfully in several key defence electronics markets where Raytheon is not a significant participant."
Raytheon and Texas Instrument's Defence Systems & Electronics Group both manufacture missiles, sensors and seekers and aircraft and ground radar, but do not overlap, analysts said.

Texas Instruments' defence unit, based in Lewisville, Texas, supplies advanced defence systems, including precision-guided weapons, strike missiles, airborne radar, night vision systems and electronic warfare systems.
The unit has about 12,000 employees and is expected to have 1996 revenues of about $1.8 billion.
Raytheon is a leader in air-to-air and ship-defence missiles, ground-based and shipboard radar, and has a major but weakening presence in missile defence systems such as the Patriot programme.
Texas Instruments President and Chief Executive Thomas Engibous said in a statement the sale would allow his company to focus on "digital solutions for the networked society."
Raytheon said the acquisition is not expected to affect earnings per share this year and should "provide increasingly positive contributions to earnings per share thereafter."
The deal would raise the Lexington, Mass.-based company's total debt to more than $6.6 billion, which Raytheon spokesman Robert McWade said it plans to pay off in five years.
The sale has been approved by the boards of both companies, and is expected to close in the 1997 second quarter, subject to government antitrust review.
Analysts welcomed the merger.
"They're just so complementary in all their programmes. They just duplicate each other," said one analyst, who requested anonymity. "It would be nicely monopolistic in short-range missiles."
Still, some analysts said the price may be too high.

"On the surface, it appears that they are paying a pretty hefty premium," said another analyst, who also asked not to be identified. "I think it probably strategically is a good fit, but if you grossly overpaid ..."
Raytheon likely paid the high price to give it a step up in the expected bidding for General Motors Corp.'s Hughes Electronics Corp., analysts said.

The first analyst said Raytheon likely paid the hefty amount in order to conduct a cash rather than a stock deal, which would complicate a Raytheon stock bid for Hughes, he said. The Raytheon spokesman declined to say if Raytheon was a suitor for Hughes.
Northrop Grumman Corp. is expected to be Raytheon's only competitor in the bidding for Hughes.

Raytheon has been a major player in the consolidation of the defence industry. In April 1995 it acquired E-Systems for more than $2 billion and a year later it bought Chrysler Corp.'s defence-electronics business for $475 million.
Texas Instruments' stock rose $2 to $68.875, while Raytheon gained 62.5 cents to $50.625, both on the New York Stock Exchange in late-morning trading.
